{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement UI behavior and client-side request patterns that match the server access rules below. Do not assume any server behavior beyond what is specified. Use the concrete HTTP responses to drive UI state.

Assumptions you may use in client code: currentAuthenticatedUser (id and whether they are the local client’s user) is available; endpoints follow the pattern {resourceBase}/{id} for single-resource GET/PUT/DELETE and {resourceBase} for POST.

Required UI behaviors and client logic:

1) Fetch/display resource (GET {resourceBase}/{id})
- If response is 200: render the resource.
  - If currentAuthenticatedUser.id === resource.owner_id: render editable view (show Edit and Delete controls, inputs enabled).
  - Else (currentAuthenticatedUser is not owner): render read-only view (inputs disabled, hide or disable Edit and Delete controls).
    - Note: the only case a non-owner will get 200 is when the server allows read for superusers; the client must not itself infer role-based semantics beyond comparing owner_id.
- If response is 404: treat as “Not found” — show standard Not Found UI (do not render read-only content). Do not reveal whether resource existed or whether it was forbidden.
- If response is 403: (server may only return 403 for write attempts per backend contract) show an appropriate error message and remain on the current view; do not treat GET 403 as authorized read.

2) Create resource (POST {resourceBase})
- Do not send owner_id in the request body. The server will set owner_id to the current user on creation.
- If server returns 201 (or 200 per existing API), fetch the created resource for display. Verify resource.owner_id equals currentAuthenticatedUser.id when showing the resource.
- If server returns 4xx/5xx, surface the returned error to the user.

3) Update resource (PUT {resourceBase}/{id})
- Only enable the Update action and editable inputs if currentAuthenticatedUser.id === resource.owner_id.
- Always remove/ignore any owner_id key from the outgoing update payload (do not attempt to change owner_id).
- If a PUT returns 200/204, update UI accordingly.
- If a PUT returns 403 with JSON body exactly containing {"detail":"Read-only access"}: present a clear message that the resource is read-only and revert UI to read-only (disable inputs and hide Update/Delete). Do not attempt further write retries without user action.
- If a PUT returns 404: navigate to/show Not Found UI.

4) Delete resource (DELETE {resourceBase}/{id})
- Only show/enable Delete if currentAuthenticatedUser.id === resource.owner_id.
- If DELETE returns 204/200: remove the resource from the UI (navigate to list or confirmation).
- If DELETE returns 403 with JSON body {"detail":"Read-only access"}: show a message that deletion is not allowed (read-only) and switch to read-only view.
- If DELETE returns 404: show Not Found UI.

5) Error handling and messaging
- Explicitly handle and check for 403 responses whose body equals {"detail":"Read-only access"} and treat them as enforced read-only for the current resource.
- Do not convert server 404 for others’ resources into a local “forbidden”; show “Not found” per server response.

6) Tests and acceptance checks (client-side end-to-end)
- Superuser viewing own resource: GET returns 200; inputs editable; Update/Delete succeed.
- Superuser viewing another user’s resource: GET returns 200; inputs disabled; Update and Delete buttons hidden; if a write is attempted (simulated), server returns 403 with {"detail":"Read-only access"} and UI shows read-only message and disables edit controls.
- Normal user viewing another user’s resource: GET returns 404 and UI shows Not Found.
- Nonexistent resource: GET/PUT/DELETE return 404 and UI shows Not Found.
- Create: POST without owner_id; after creation, GET shows owner_id === currentAuthenticatedUser.id.

Implementation notes for developers integrating with the backend:
- Rely only on server status codes and bodies described above. Do not assume additional fields or headers beyond the described JSON error body for the 403 case.
- Keep owner_id out of client-sent create/update payloads.
"
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement server-side access control and responses exactly as described below. Do not assume any behavior not specified here. Use the resource identifier {id} and endpoints: GET /{resourceBase}/{id}, PUT /{resourceBase}/{id}, DELETE /{resourceBase}/{id}, POST /{resourceBase}.

Preconditions/assumptions you may use in server code: request.user is the authenticated user object; request.user.id is the user id; request.user.is_superuser indicates superuser status. If your platform represents these differently, map accordingly, but preserve the semantics.

Access rules (must be enforced for every relevant endpoint):
1) GET /{resourceBase}/{id}
- If resource with id does not exist -> return 404.
- If request.user.id === resource.owner_id -> return 200 with resource payload.
- Else if request.user.is_superuser -> return 200 with resource payload (superuser may read others’ resources).
- Else -> return 404. (Normal users must not learn the resource exists.)

2) PUT /{resourceBase}/{id}
- If resource with id does not exist -> return 404.
- If request.user.id === resource.owner_id -> perform the update and return 200 or 204 per existing API.
  - When applying updates, ignore any owner_id present in the request body; preserve the current owner_id.
- Else if request.user.is_superuser -> do NOT allow write. Return 403 with JSON body exactly {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
- Else -> return 404.

3) DELETE /{resourceBase}/{id}
- If resource with id does not exist -> return 404.
- If request.user.id === resource.owner_id -> delete and return 204 or 200 per existing API.
- Else if request.user.is_superuser -> do NOT allow delete. Return 403 with JSON body exactly {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
- Else -> return 404.

4) POST /{resourceBase}
- Create a new resource. Ignore any owner_id provided by the client; set resource.owner_id = request.user.id before saving.
- Return 201 (or existing API success code) and the created resource.

Error body requirements
- For the superuser write-block case, the response body must be JSON and exactly include detail set to the string "Read-only access". Example: {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
- For 404 responses and other error responses, use existing API formats; do not change response formats for non-specified cases.

Acceptance tests (automated) to add/verify on the backend:
- Superuser reads another user’s resource: GET returns 200 with resource.
- Superuser attempts to PUT or DELETE another user’s resource: returns 403 with body {"detail":"Read-only access"} and resource remains unchanged.
- Superuser can PUT/DELETE their own resource: operations succeed.
- Normal user attempts to GET another user’s resource: returns 404.
- Any user attempts GET/PUT/DELETE for non-existent id: returns 404.
- POST with owner_id in payload: server ignores provided owner_id and persists owner_id = request.user.id; verify via GET of created resource.

Implementation notes and safe defaults
- Do not return 403 for normal users trying to access others’ resources — return 404 to avoid information leakage.
- Ensure that any attempt to change owner_id during update is ignored (preserve existing owner) or rejected consistently; document which behavior you choose. If you choose to reject on attempted owner_id change, return 400 with an explanatory message (but do not rely on that for frontend logic; the frontend should simply avoid sending owner_id).
- Log enforced Read-only events for audit but do not expose logs to clients.

Do not implement any access behavior beyond these rules or rely on unstated headers or tokens. Ensure the exact 403 JSON body for superuser write attempts to allow the frontend to detect and present the read-only state."
  }
}
